summary: Vocabulary/naming guidance for ages 7–9 on changes of state and separation: dissolve, solution, mixture, soluble/insoluble, melt, freeze, evaporate, condense, filter, sieve, separate. The central teaching goal is to tie each process word to the visible action it names and to keep 'dissolve' and 'melt' distinct (the single most confused pair), while teaching verbs as reversible/opposite pairs (dissolve–recover, mix–separate, melt–freeze, evaporate–condense) and distinguishing a solution (a clear, uniform mixture) from a mixture in general. Preserves a primary observation-anchored activity plus matching, use-in-context, and a reversible/irreversible transfer check with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: Dissolving and melting are treated as the same thing ('the sugar melted in the water').
A dissolved solid is thought to be destroyed or to have vanished, rather than spread through the liquid.
'Mixture' and 'solution' are used interchangeably without noticing a solution is clear/uniform.
Filtering and sieving are conflated, without linking each to what property (particle size) it exploits.
Evaporate and condense are seen as unrelated rather than opposite directions of the same change.

activities.title: Changes bench: name the process you can see
steps: Observe (in real life, a short clip, or a labelled picture scene) several changes side by side: sugar stirred into a glass of water, an ice cube melting on a saucer, chocolate softening on a warm plate, muddy water poured through a funnel-and-filter, and a puddle drying in the sun.
For each one, say aloud the process word that names what is happening (dissolve, melt, filter, evaporate) and, where possible, hear or repeat its pronunciation.

For the sugar-in-water and the chocolate, answer the key prompt: 'What did the solid become?' — the sugar broke into tiny bits spread invisibly through the water, making a solution (a clear, uniform mixture in which the sugar is still present but too small to see); the chocolate turned into a puddle of liquid.
State the partner/opposite word for each change: melt–freeze, mix–separate, evaporate–condense, dissolve–recover.
Give evidence the dissolved sugar is still present (e.g. with food-safe sugar in clean water it still tastes sweet; evaporating the water leaves the sugar behind).
activities.insight: Each process word names a specific visible action; dissolving (a solid spreading invisibly through a liquid to form a solution — a clear, uniform mixture) is different from melting (a solid turning to liquid on warming), and many of these changes come in reversible pairs.

activities.title: Word-to-action matching and use-in-context
steps: Match each process word (dissolve, melt, filter, sieve, evaporate, condense, freeze) to the picture or short description of the action it names.

Where feasible as a hands-on 'do-it' moment, stir a soluble solid (e.g. sugar) into water and say 'dissolving' as it happens; then describe the result with 'solution' and 'mixture', noting that a solution is a clear, uniform kind of mixture in which the separate solid can no longer be seen. For contrast, stir an insoluble solid (e.g. sand) into water and see that it stays visible and does not dissolve, making a mixture that is not a solution. Name each solid as soluble or insoluble.
Pair each matched word with its opposite/partner word to confirm it is learned as part of a reversible pair.
activities.insight: Using the vocabulary actively — matching, labelling, and speaking it during the action — consolidates the meaning; matching alone checks recognition, while narrating during the action elicits the learner's own production.

activities.title: Reversible vs irreversible sorting check
steps: Given examples that include reversible changes (melting ice, dissolving sugar, freezing water, evaporating a puddle) and at least one clearly irreversible change (e.g. cooking an egg or burning paper), sort which changes can be undone and name the word for undoing each reversible one.
Apply a separation word ('evaporate', 'filter') correctly to a new case not seen during teaching.
activities.insight: The process vocabulary can be transferred to new situations and used to judge whether a change can be reversed.

checkQuestion: You've just watched me stir sugar into warm water until it vanishes, and separately watched an ice lolly go soft and drippy on the table. Talk me through what happened at each one — tell it to a friend who wasn't here, using your best 'what-happened' words.
checkAnswer: For the sugar: it DISSOLVED — the sugar and water made a SOLUTION (a MIXTURE), the sugar is still there, spread out too small to see. For the lolly: it MELTED — a solid turned to liquid because it warmed up. A strong answer keeps 'dissolve' and 'melt' apart, and uses 'mixture'/'solution' for the sugar-water and 'melt' for the state change.
